methodological_rigor.justification: This retrospective study assembled a large real-world cohort of HER2-negative metastatic gastric cancer treated with first-line PD-1 blockade-based therapy and split it into training (n = 714) and validation (n = 180) cohorts. Prognostic factors were identified via univariate and multivariate Cox regression and incorporated into a nomogram, with discrimination and calibration assessed using time-dependent ROC/AUCs, calibration plots, and bootstrap resampling (1000 resamples). Key limitations are inherent to the single-center retrospective design and the absence of true external validation, which the manuscript acknowledges. Several potentially important molecular variables (e.g., PD-L1 CPS, EBV DNA, TMB) were not incorporated due to high missingness (>50%), which may introduce residual confounding and limits model completeness.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The work is an observational prognostic study in a defined clinical cohort of metastatic gastric cancer patients receiving contemporary first-line PD-1 blockade-based regimens, consistent with an Oxford LoE of 2b (individual cohort study). Clinical relevance is high because it targets outcomes that matter to patients (PFS and OS) and proposes an easy-to-use risk stratification tool using routinely available baseline variables (ECOG PS, metastatic pattern, Lauren type, CRP, LDH). The manuscript reports that intermediate- and high-risk groups had significantly worse PFS/OS than the low-risk group in both training and validation cohorts (all P < 0.001) and that stratification associated with disease control rate. However, generalizability to other centers and treatment mixes remains uncertain without external validation.

reporting_quality.justification: This is a prognostic model/nomogram paper, so TRIPOD is the most applicable reporting standard; the manuscript describes cohort dates (October 2018 to July 2024), a train/validation split, predictor selection via Cox regression, and model performance using ROC/AUCs, calibration, and decision curve analysis. It also transparently notes major constraints (single-center retrospective design and lack of external validation) and reports substantial missingness for molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 CPS missing in >50%). Some key reproducibility elements remain limited in the normalized text (e.g., full model specification/handling of missing data beyond excluding sparsely available markers), and many details are referenced to supplementary materials and a dynamic nomogram website that are redacted here. No clear public data or code repository is described in the manuscript text provided.

novelty_literature.justification: The manuscript's novelty is primarily empirical and applied: it develops a prognostic nomogram specifically for HER2-negative metastatic gastric cancer patients receiving first-line PD-1 blockade-based therapy using a comparatively large real-world cohort. The variables and modeling approach (clinicopathologic predictors plus Cox regression-based nomogram) are standard, and the contribution is more a setting-specific calibration and risk stratification than a new mechanism or method. The paper positions the nomogram against PD-L1 CPS and several previously reported scores via ROC/DCA comparisons, suggesting incremental improvement in prognostic discrimination in this treatment context. Without external validation and with excluded molecular predictors due to missingness, the advance is meaningful but not field-defining.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract clearly states the clinical problem, retrospective design, cohort sizes (714/180), statistical approach (Cox models, time-dependent ROC, calibration, DCA), and the resulting risk stratification tied to PFS/OS. Methods and results are presented in a logical flow from factor identification to model construction and validation, with figures/tables described (Kaplan-Meier curves, nomogram, ROC/calibration plots). Limitations are explicitly discussed (single-center retrospective design, missing molecular markers, and need for external/prospective validation). Some interpretive claims (e.g., comparisons to other models) lean on supplementary materials that are not fully visible in this normalized corpus.

key_strengths: Large real-world cohort with an internal validation split (training n = 714; validation n = 180) in a contemporary first-line PD-1 blockade-treated population.
Use of multivariable Cox modeling and multiple performance checks (time-dependent ROC/AUCs, calibration, decision curve analyses, bootstrap resampling) to support the nomogram.
Clinically accessible predictors (ECOG PS, metastatic pattern, Lauren type, CRP, LDH) enabling pragmatic risk stratification linked to PFS/OS and disease control.
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective design without true external validation limits generalizability and raises selection-bias concerns.
High missingness for key biomarkers (e.g., PD-L1 CPS, EBV DNA, TMB) leading to their exclusion and potentially limiting model completeness and transportability.
Potential overfitting and optimism from data-driven cutpoints (X-tile-derived thresholds) and lack of clarity on missing-data handling for included variables in the visible text.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a solid, clinically oriented prognostic model with strong internal validation signals, but the lack of external validation and substantial missingness for important biomarkers keep it below top-tier acceptance. At a mid-tier journal level, major revisions focused on TRIPOD completeness and validation/transportability would be expected.
